findings: S2 has the sign backwards on account 4100, service revenue. The table runs $1,096,000 to $1,014,000, a decline of $82,000 or 7.5 percent. The sentence says it grew $82,000 on maintenance contract renewals, so the only driver offered explains a movement that went the other way. A territory losing $82,000 of recurring service revenue needs a real explanation, and none is here.

S4 misstates the amount on account 6050, temporary labor. $121,400 less $34,600 is $86,800, not the $68,800 the sentence claims. The digits are transposed and $18,000 of the increase disappears from the narrative. The percent in the table, 250.9 percent, is computed off the correct $86,800, so the prose and the table disagree with each other.

S8 misstates the amount on account 7100, interest expense. $88,600 less $76,300 is $12,300. The sentence says $16,100, which is the 16.1 percent figure rewritten with a dollar sign. $16,100 appears nowhere in the table. Separately, a revolver draw to fund inventory should show up as higher average borrowings, and nothing here ties the $12,300 to a draw amount or a rate.

S11 is arithmetically false on accounts 4000 and 5000. July product gross margin is $5,398,000 less $4,131,000 over $5,398,000, which is 23.5 percent. August is $5,905,000 less $4,612,000 over $5,905,000, which is 21.9 percent. They are not both 22 percent rounded. Margin fell roughly 160 basis points, about $93,000 of gross profit at August volume, and the conclusion that channel mix did not move is drawn from a number that does not exist.

Account 5000, cost of product sold, moved $481,000 or 11.6 percent and is marked over threshold, yet no sentence in the commentary explains it. Revenue on 4000 rose 9.4 percent while cost rose 11.6 percent. That gap is the single most important thing in the file and it is unaddressed.

Account 4300, supplier rebates, moved $172,000 or 409.5 percent and is marked over threshold, and there is no commentary on it at all. A jump from $42,000 to $214,000 in one month reads as a catch-up or a true-up rather than a run rate. I need to know the period the rebate relates to, because if it is earning from prior months it does not belong in August, and $172,000 of other income is enough to change how the month reads.

S5 attaches the driver to the wrong account. Inbound freight, account 5100, rose $27,600 or 11.3 percent, and the sentence explains it with the temporary labor added at Northgate. Temp labor is a warehouse cost in account 6050 and cannot cause inbound carrier charges. Inbound freight moves with purchase volume, lane mix, or carrier rates, and cost of product sold rose 11.6 percent in the same month, which is the obvious place to look.

S9 and S10 cannot both be true. S9 says no new legal matters arose in August, while account 7300 carries a new $185,000 settlement accrual that was zero in July. A $185,000 charge is a new matter by any reading, and one of these two sentences has to be withdrawn.

S10 puts the $185,000 in account 7300 in the wrong period and then describes it wrongly. If the delivery claim was resolved in June, the loss was probable and estimable in June and the accrual belongs there, which makes this a prior period item rather than an August cost. Calling it something that reverses once the release is signed is also wrong. A settlement accrual is relieved by payment, not reversed, and if it truly reverses then it was never a settlement.

S6 describes an unrecorded liability and leaves it unrecorded. Three August invoices totaling $31,200 for fuel and freight sat in September because the vendor portal closed. That is a cutoff error, not a narrative point. August accounts 5100 and 6100 are both understated, the $31,200 appears nowhere in the table, and the fix is an accrual before this book closes.

The $31,200 in S6 also breaks the threshold determination on account 6100, fleet fuel. As shown, fuel moved $6,200 or 5.7 percent and escapes commentary. Push any material share of $31,200 back into August and the movement can clear the $25,000 test, which means the commentary list itself was built off understated numbers.

S3 claims a productivity program on account 6000, warehouse wages, but the two labor lines together say otherwise. Wages fell $37,700 while temporary labor rose $86,800, so total warehouse labor went from $816,500 to $865,600, up $49,100 or 6.0 percent. That pattern is people moving from payroll to agency, not productivity. A program launched at the start of the month delivering 4.8 percent in its first month would be unusual in any case.

S7 spends three clauses, a reserve percentage and a payment plan on account 6400, bad debt expense, for a $1,700 movement, while $481,000 on account 5000 and $172,000 on account 4300 get nothing. The effort is inverted. I would also want the receivable balance behind that $1,700, because a 15 percent reserve on a single account moving past ninety days implies roughly $11,000 of exposure and that is not worth a sentence either.

S12 is a sentence spent to report that account 6700, insurance, was flat at $47,300 and requires no comment. The identical dollar in both months is worth one question, whether the policy is on straight amortization or the accrual simply was not trued up, but as written the line adds nothing while material accounts stay silent.

S1 asserts share gains in the independent restaurant channel on account 4000 with nothing behind it. Revenue rose $507,000 or 9.4 percent, the largest dollar movement in the file, and cost of product sold rose faster at 11.6 percent. Share bought with price concessions looks exactly like this, and the sentence should carry volume and price separately before anyone signs it.

The threshold policy itself lets the two biggest revenue movements through untouched. Account 4000 moved $507,000 at 9.4 percent and account 4100 moved $82,000 at 7.5 percent, so $589,000 of revenue movement clears the dollar test and fails the percent test and requires no comment. Account 7300 has no percent at all because the prior month is zero, yet it is marked over threshold, so the rule is being applied inconsistently in both directions.
